headline: Bond Selloff Resumes as Fed Hike Bets Firm Up
tileReason: Bond markets reopened today after Veterans Day and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back above 5% as traders lock in a December Fed hike, adding pressure to a daily 30-year average already at 7.30%.
takeaway:
Rates start today under fresh pressure. The daily 30-year average last stood at 7.30% after Tuesday's jump from 7.18%, and with bond markets closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, today is the first trading session since then. Today's index posts this afternoon, and early bond trading points to lenders pricing a bit higher, not lower.

The 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%. The yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, was trading around 5.02% to 5.08% this morning, depending on the source and time, up from about 4.98% at Tuesday's close. That is the move Treasury futures, which kept trading through the holiday, had hinted at Wednesday.

Traders now see a December Fed hike as close to a sure thing. After Tuesday's hot inflation report, the CME FedWatch tool, which converts futures prices into odds, puts the chance of a Dec 9 hike at roughly 91% to 100% depending on how outlets report it, with a small chance it is a half point. Markets also expect more increases early next year, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee has described the inflation report as deeply troubling.

This morning's news was mixed. Weekly jobless claims rose to 200,000, a bit more than forecasters expected but still low, and existing home sales fell 5.5% in October to a 3.75 million yearly pace, weaker than expected. Oil slipped overnight on hopes for Iran and Ukraine peace talks, then turned higher after President Trump said the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran, leaving Brent crude near $92 to $93 a barrel. Stocks fell after Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, but that has not pulled yields lower so far.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff, and it leaves space for mortgage rates to improve if markets settle.

The next tests come fast. Freddie Mac's weekly rate survey comes out at noon Eastern today, the Treasury sells $25 billion of 30-year bonds this afternoon after Tuesday's weak 10-year sale, and six Fed officials speak today and this evening. Friday brings October wholesale inflation (PPI), then retail sales on Nov 17, the Fed's preferred inflation measure on Nov 25, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Investing.com and CappNotes (Nov 10); CME FedWatch via Options Oracle, Trading Economics and U.Today (Nov 12); Kalshi via Options Oracle (Nov 12); The Blye Sheet and Saxo (Nov 12)
fedOdds.note: Sources differ. Options Oracle and Trading Economics put December hike odds near 91% this morning, while U.Today reported the CME FedWatch snapshot at 100%; the gap likely reflects whether the half-point chance is counted separately. The Blye Sheet says futures price about 0.29% of tightening in December, slightly more than one quarter-point hike, and Kalshi shows about 86%.

drivers.title: Hot October inflation still driving the market
drivers.text: Tuesday's report showed consumer prices up 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected, and core prices (no food or energy) up 0.3% versus 0.2%. Higher-than-expected inflation makes bond investors demand higher yields, and with Wednesday's holiday this is the first full day of cash bond trading to digest it, so the 10-year yield is back above 5% this morning.

drivers.title: Markets lock in a December Fed hike
drivers.text: Futures markets now treat a Dec 9 rate hike as close to certain, with a small chance of a half point and more increases expected by March. Chicago Fed President Goolsbee has called the inflation data deeply troubling, and six Fed officials speak today. When traders expect higher short-term rates for longer, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: 30-year bond sale after a weak 10-year sale
drivers.text: Tuesday's $42 billion 10-year sale drew its softest demand since May, and the Treasury sells $25 billion of 30-year bonds this afternoon. If buyers again need a higher yield to absorb all that new debt, long-term yields rise and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Oil swings on Iran headlines
drivers.text: Oil dipped overnight on hopes for Iran and Ukraine peace talks and higher Saudi and Iraqi output, then turned higher after President Trump said the U.S. does not need an Iran deal, with Brent near $92 to $93. Higher oil feeds into fuel and shipping costs and inflation worries, which tends to push bond yields up; it is still well below its October peak, which limits the damage.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much, and weaker housing data like today's drop in home sales can help keep pressure off.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 10 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds lean a little more toward higher rates than on Wednesday. The 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5% this morning, a December Fed hike is essentially fully expected with more priced for early next year, and demand at Tuesday's 10-year sale was weak, with a 30-year sale this afternoon. Part of that is already in Tuesday's jump to 7.30%. In borrowers' favor: mortgage rates sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.17% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), housing data are softening, and oil is well below its October peak. Big swing events: Friday's wholesale inflation report, Iran and oil headlines, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average stands at 7.30% after Tuesday's jump, and with the 10-year Treasury yield back above 5% this morning, lenders may price a little higher today. It's still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates turned higher this week after a month of easing, and October home sales fell 5.5%, so buyers are feeling the pinch. With a December Fed hike now expected, realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates are holding near 7.30% after this week's hot inflation report, and bond yields are back above 5% as markets brace for a December Fed hike.
